canberra.title: Whether you’re a green gardener or a guru, Open Gardens Canberra has inspiration aplenty
canberra.snippet: Whether you’re a raw beginner or a seasoned gardener, there’s nothing quite so addictive as looking at other people’s g...
canberra.content:
The Baker garden in Griffith is open to the public again and is more accessible in 2026. Photo: OGC.

Whether you’re a raw beginner or a seasoned gardener, there’s nothing quite so addictive as looking at other people’s gardens.

They’re a fertile source of inspiration, design ideas and straightforward knowledge about what will (or won’t) grow in our neck of the woods. That latter point is critically important in Canberra, where our seasonal conditions are quite different and often a fair bit tougher than coastal Australia – so where better to learn about what does well than from the neighbours?

This spring, the Open Gardens Canberra programme includes nine varied gardens (with more to come in autumn), each demonstrating the skills and imagination Canberra gardeners have in abundance.

The Forrest Bower is a two-in-one garden, enabling two quite different but complementary approaches to flourish. A leafy green, restrained and restful garden surrounds the original area, while the block next door takes advantage of a different space to create a more colourful, vibrant plant palette and landscaping. The garden is open on September 19 and 20.

Late in September, garden visitors can be inspired by years of dedication in the Garden of Memories at Lyons. This 60-year-old garden demonstrates all the benefits of maturity, as well as the complexities of renewal and rejuvenation.

Sited atop a large block with sweeping valley views, the garden has new landscaping and eclectic planting to complement the established structure. It opens on the weekend of September 26 and 27.

There’s a last chance to visit a couple of favourite Canberra gardens this spring: the Baker garden in Griffith is beautifully maintained and has been recently modified for easier access and maintenance, an important consideration for older gardeners in particular. It’s open on October 3 and 4.

Els’ Garden in Flynn. Photo: OGC.

Els’ Garden in Flynn is unusually large with a backyard creek, extensive native plantings and a wisteria-covered pergola. Don’t miss it on 10-11 October.

And if you’re considering how to manage some acres, the Vogelweide Estate in Gundaroo is outstanding. The gardens draw their inspiration from European planting beneath a well-established tree canopy, with masses of heavenly roses and peonies, and a traditional herbaceous border demonstrating real skill. The Vogelweide estate is open on 24-25 October.

Canberra is a green city with garden suburbs that were a key part of the city’s original plan. Garden By Fleur in Braddon, which opens on 31 October-1 November, surrounds a multigenerational family home. The professional design is a masterclass in making the best use of an average-sized block and suits family living.

As spring reaches its peak in early November, don’t miss the restful and much-loved Joan’s Garden in Fadden on 7-8 November. Garden lovers may have previously seen this green and restful garden in its autumn finery and can now enjoy spring-flowering planting and a secluded pond.

Sustainability is a key driver for many establishing new gardens, and when Zhou’s Sustainable Kitchen Garden opens on 21-22 November in Kambah, visitors can explore an entire suburban block dedicated to sustainable and organic gardening. The garden includes a thriving orchard with a huge variety of fruit trees, berry bushes, herbs and productive edible plants of every kind.

The restful and much-loved Joan’s Garden in Fadden has evolved over the years. Photo: OGC.

On the same weekend, the Secret Country Garden in Waramanga is a beautifully layered Australian garden blending formal structure with relaxed cottage planting, and featuring abundant spring colour, tranquil outdoor rooms alive with birdlife and secluded sitting areas.

Garden entries from the 2025-26 program funded horticulture scholarships, and grants to support community projects. Funding for new projects is currently in train and will be announced shortly.

Membership of Open Gardens Canberra at $30 per annum gives you free entry to all OGC gardens for the whole financial year. If you’d like to help, volunteers are essential to opening the gardens and are always needed and welcome.

Contact info@opengardenscanberra.org.au for more information about the program and membership.

canberra.title: ‘Exceeding’ but under investigation: Why top childcare ratings don’t always tell parents the full story
canberra.snippet: An ‘Exceeding National Quality Standard’ rating is supposed to signal one of the country’s highest-performing childcare...
canberra.content:
8 August 2026

Start the conversation

Edge Early Learning at Higgins scored an ‘Exceeding’ rating despite compliance action. Photo: Region.

An ‘Exceeding National Quality Standard’ rating is supposed to signal one of the country’s highest-performing childcare services.

But ACT officials have acknowledged a centre can retain that rating even while it is the subject of serious regulatory investigations.

The issue came under scrutiny during Budget Estimates after independent MLA Thomas Emerson questioned why Edge Early Learning Higgins continued to display an ‘Exceeding’ rating despite repeated compliance action and a four-week emergency closure.

Mr Emerson told the hearing parents had raised concerns about a series of incidents at the centre over recent years, including allegations that a child had climbed onto a roof, another child had been found with a cord around their neck, a child had their hair cut with scissors and, most recently, a child was allegedly given food they were known to be allergic to.

He questioned whether a parent looking at the centre’s quality rating would have any indication those matters had been investigated.

Education Directorate executive branch manager Sean Moysey said the answer lay in the way Australia’s childcare regulatory system is designed.

A National Quality Standard rating and compliance action are two separate regulatory processes.

A quality rating reflects a service’s performance at the time it is formally assessed against seven quality areas, including children’s health and safety, educational programs, staffing, leadership and governance.

Compliance investigations, on the other hand, respond to specific incidents or alleged breaches that occur after that assessment and do not automatically trigger a reassessment or change to a centre’s published rating.

Mr Moysey acknowledged the situation created what he described as a “conundrum” for regulators.

On the one hand, he said, it would be inappropriate to change a service’s quality rating simply because an investigation had commenced before findings were made.

On the other hand, he accepted that parents could reasonably expect a highly rated service to reflect its current circumstances.

“It’s something we’re working through nationally,” Mr Moysey told the committee, referring to discussions between regulators about whether the current framework gives families the clearest picture when choosing childcare.

The hearing also raised questions about delays in the ACT introduction of a public register on childcare enforcement information. Mr Emerson highlighted that other states including Queensland, Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia have already introduced them.

Mr Moysey confirmed the ACT remained “on track” to establish its own register but said officials wanted to ensure it aligned with information already available through the national StartingBlocks website rather than duplicate it.

“It’s a logistical issue,” he said.

“One of the things we want to make sure is what we put on the register locally aligns with what’s on the register nationally.”

The register is expected to give parents easier access to compliance information while also providing context about the significance of different regulatory actions, recognising that not every compliance notice reflects the same level of risk. Officials also said guidance would be developed to help families understand what questions to ask when choosing a childcare provider.

The move follows national reforms introduced earlier this year that expanded the information available to families through the Australian Government’s StartingBlocks website, which now publishes a range of enforcement actions taken by state and territory regulators over the previous two years. Those reforms were introduced to improve transparency and help parents make more informed decisions when selecting childcare.

canberra.title: The Pacific Food Studio is serving big flavours from a tiny Kingston kitchen
canberra.snippet: A few blocks from the buzz of the Kingston Foreshore, tucked into the Parbery Street precinct, sits The Pacific Food Studio. It is a lite...
canberra.content:
Slow-cooked pork nachos. Photo: Sophia Brady.

A few blocks from the buzz of the Kingston Foreshore, tucked into the Parbery Street precinct, sits The Pacific Food Studio.

It is a literal hole in the wall overlooking a courtyard lined with picnic tables. If I had not been taking my dogs to the vet around the corner, I may never have found it.

That would have been a huge shame because some serious magic is coming out of this tiny kitchen.

Drawn in by the intoxicating aroma of lunch service, I grabbed an outdoor table on a sunny winter afternoon, dogs in tow. My stomach refused to let me leave without succumbing to whatever was cooking behind that window and finding out more about the two friendly faces who had been running it for the past three months.

Chef Alejandro Torres Santelices has spent much of the past 15 years cooking in some of Canberra’s most notable kitchens.

Since arriving from Chile in 2011, he has worked at Jamala Wildlife Lodge, the Embassy of Mexico, Government House and the High Commission of Canada, cooking a variety of cuisines and catering for diplomats and dignitaries.

Now, together with partner Lee Vu, who comes from a very active foodie family, they are bringing those experiences together in a business of their own. Rather than opening a large restaurant, the pair chose to keep things compact, from the menu to the venue, naming it after the ocean between Australia and the Americas.

“The Pacific covers a vast range of civilisations and flavours. I want to show Aussies what is happening throughout that area, especially the vibrant Spanish-speaking cultures of the Americas, through food,” Alejandro says.

“Growing up in Chile, I came from a family of cooks, and that, along with working with so many brilliant chefs from around the world, has kept my curiosity for food so active. It now shapes what appears on the menu daily.”

Owners Alejandro Torres Santelices and Lee Vu. Photo: Sophia Brady

For lunch, I ordered the slow-cooked pork nachos, which arrived loaded with tender pork shoulder braised for hours with achiote, a native Mexican seed. The meat was deeply savoury, incredibly moist and simply excellent.

Piled on top was guacamole and a very satisfying addition of feta cheese and pickled onions. It was served with two salsas, a vibrant tomatillo and a spicy red chilli. It caught me off guard how much I enjoyed this seemingly simple dish; it was surprisingly layered and thoughtfully balanced.

The meal was memorable enough that I found myself thinking about it afterwards, so I decided to work my way through more of the menu. I popped back in to pick up a takeaway dinner order of chicken and chorizo paella, a selection of empanadas, another serve of the pork nachos and a side of fries, which only strengthened my first impression that I had stumbled onto something special.

The paella was mouthwatering to look at and absolutely delicious, one of the best I have had in Canberra. The golden crust on the bottom was spot on, the chicken pieces juicy and tender, the chorizo providing a nice bit of fat, and even the green beans, an ingredient I would normally avoid, earned their place on my fork. The rice was cooked through perfectly, and the beautiful blend of paprika and saffron came through in every bite.

The golden crust on the bottom of the paella was spot on. Photo: Sophia Brady.

As for the rest of the meal, the nachos were just as good the second time around, while the fries were perfectly cooked and seasoned with salt and oregano. They were impossible not to scoff by the handful. It feels silly to say, but the humble chip was a highlight.

Alejandro says quality fresh ingredients are central to everything coming out of the kitchen. He shops constantly, always keeps stocks on the boil and regularly visits markets and fishmongers to source produce.

He sums up his philosophy in four words. “Simple food properly done.”

The Pacific Food Studio is located at Shop LG 05/10 Parbery St, in Kingston. Open Tuesday to Sunday for lunch from 10:30 am to 3 pm, and dinner from 5 pm to 9 pm. Follow them on Facebook and Instagram to keep up to date with their offerings.

canberra.title: Lennox Gardens’ changing canopy as work starts to replace ageing trees
canberra.snippet: Work to remove ageing and diseased trees from Lennox Gardens in Yarralumla by Lake Burley Griffin has begun, as part of plans for a safer...
canberra.content:
8 August 2026

Start the conversation

Dozens of trees across Lennox Gardens will need to be removed. Photo: ACT Government.

Work to remove ageing and diseased trees from Lennox Gardens in Yarralumla by Lake Burley Griffin has begun, as part of plans for a safer, healthier and more resilient urban forest.

The City and Environment Directorate said 43 trees have been identified for removal and replacement over the coming weeks, but the Gardens would remain open throughout.

It said these trees were near the end of their life, structurally compromised, in poor health, dead or in decline.

They would be replaced with species better suited to the site.

Senior director urban treescapes at the City and Environment Directorate, Rachael Dawes, said the work was a necessary part of maintaining the park and renewing it for future visitors.

“While this will be a significant change for one of Canberra’s most iconic lakeside destinations, it is an important investment in the future of Lennox Gardens,” she said.

“Replacing these ageing and declining trees will help create a healthier, more resilient and diverse tree canopy that can be enjoyed by generations of Canberrans to come.”

In Canberra Nara Peace Park, replanting would reflect a traditional Japanese garden style, guided by a plan developed in partnership with the Friends of Nara Park.

The peninsula area would be replanted with a mix of conifer species to improve canopy diversity and resilience.

Friends of Canberra-Nara Peace Park convenor Dr Chris Braddick said it was sad to see these old trees go.

“It is sad to see the removal of the historic stands of moribund Himalayan Cyprus from Canberra-Nara Peace Park,” he said.

“However, future generations of park visitors will doubtless enjoy observing as the successor Japanese Black and White Pines mature into majestic trees.”

Wood harvested from the removal of the trees in Lennox Gardens will be reused as timber or mulch for government and community projects.

This would help divert material from waste streams and maximise the ongoing community and environmental value of removed trees.

Lennox Gardens will remain open during the works, with temporary access restrictions and minor detours for pedestrians and cyclists.

canberra.title: Decision on Hume Circle development proposal stinks of secrecy
canberra.snippet: The decision by the Federal Government to approve radical high-rise development at Hume Circle is further proof that Labor takes Canberra...
canberra.content:
Claire Miles is supporting the call for a Parliamentary inquiry into the approval process around the Hume Circle Precinct. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The decision by the Federal Government to approve radical high-rise development at Hume Circle is further proof that Labor takes Canberra voters for granted.

Rather than protecting an established residential neighbourhood, DA102 places existing homes under an NCA planning framework that residents fear prioritises future development over the people who already live there.

After months of community meetings, discussions with residents of Staffordshire Terrace and a public inquiry, one fundamental question was left unanswered: Why does the section of land on Hume Circle containing established homes need to be included?

NCA Chief Executive Karen Doran has maintained that it is necessary for “geometry”. Yet geometry is not a circle or a square. Geometry describes the size, shape and position of objects and, in planning terms, the boundaries of a development area.

By that logic, the boundaries could just as easily have been drawn to exclude existing properties. Instead, they have been defined in a way that captures established homes and communities.

It leaves the impression that our elected representatives are relying on the complexity of planning processes and bureaucratic language to obscure the real impact of this decision.

It is hard to avoid the conclusion that this complexity benefits those making the decision, while making it more difficult for the public to see why so many residents are devastated by the outcome.

So let’s break it down simply:

  1. Federal Territories Minister Kristy McBain has just approved Development Application 102 (DA102) for the Hume Circle Precinct. This is the area with the large roundabout where the suburbs of Kingston, Narrabundah, Fyshwick and Griffith meet at the start of Canberra Avenue.
  2. The approval for 15-storey high-rises comes after the government was approached by developers, the Jega Consortium. The stink of ACT Labor that led to the resignation of minister Yvette Berry last week is still fouling the air, and now Federal Labor is adding to the odour. It is vital for complete transparency about the Labor Party’s entanglements and connections to the consortium.
  3. The announcement has blindsided residents because the government has refused to release the documents detailing how and why the decision was made. The approval for new development has been protested by locals, as it will dramatically change their suburbs, turn the area into the most densely populated part of Canberra, and stretch infrastructure and resources to breaking point.
  4. Some small changes to the original plans to quieten community concerns do not go far enough, and the issues raised by locals have been given little more than lip service. There is no genuine consultation or transparency, and the Federal Government has given homeowners no clear or lasting protections.

Effectively, the residents of Kingston, Narrabundah and Griffith woke up to discover the future of their neighbourhoods, homes and lifestyle
have been decided in secret by a minister who doesn’t live in the ACT, but met with developers behind closed doors.

They have also been betrayed by local Labor MPs who have ignored their cries for help and refuse to demand that the government release all documents connected with the decision.

Meeting with locals over the past eight months, it is clear they were frustrated, angry and worried about the development proposal. Based on the many dozens of calls and emails I’ve received since the announcement, those feelings have turned into heartbreak and a complete loss of trust.

Residents have spent months challenging the National Capital Authority (NCA) over the planning proposal, seeking transparency, meaningful consultation and lasting protections for their homes.

Yet once they were advised that DA102 was ready to be sent to the minister for approval, residents have had no opportunity to review the final version prior to its being signed.

One resident of Staffordshire Terrace summed up the issue perfectly when she told me, “our community has been left devastated. The controversy raises fundamental questions about transparency, accountability and democratic consultation”.

A resident named Kimberley wrote to me saying: “For those of us who live here, this is deeply personal. The NCA has shifted the parameters under public pressure, but residents have been given no enduring guarantee. A three-storey limit today can be changed without sign-off once our homes fall under NCA planning control. DA102 still enables towers of up to 15 storeys. An oversight committee comprising the same authorities is no substitute for independent protection.”

Residents are also questioning – quite rightly – why Canberra’s elected representatives have not demanded that the final documents be made public before such a significant planning decision was approved.

People should not have to discover the future of their neighbourhood after the decision has already been made. This is not how democracy should work.

If DA102 has nothing to hide, there is a very simple solution – release the final signed document and all associated planning material immediately.

I fully support and echo Senator David Pocock’s calls for a Parliamentary Inquiry. He is the only Federal politician fighting for the locals and for transparency and integrity on this matter.

It is clearer today than ever that electing independents is vital to holding governments to account and ensuring our voices are heard, as Labor believes there are no consequences for ignoring locals or putting the Labor Party itself ahead of the community.

Claire Miles is an independent candidate for the seat of Canberra for the 2028 Federal election.

australia.title: Sydney airport passengers warned of significant delays as dozens of flights affected
australia.snippet: Air traffic controller ‘rostering issues’ behind disruption, Airservices Australia says, with delays on more than 150 flights Get our bre...
australia.content:
Passengers travelling through the country’s largest airport have been warned of significant delays on dozens of international and domestic routes.

More than 150 flights passing through Sydney airport have been affected, including 95 across the Qantas network, as the airport struggles with staffing shortages.

Virgin flights were also affected.

A spokesperson for the airport said Airservices Australia, which oversees air traffic control there, was managing reduced air traffic movements that were expected to impact flights network-wide and result in delays.

“We encourage passengers to check with their airline for the latest information on their flight,” they said on Saturday.

Airservices Australia said it had enacted air traffic-flow management measures, including spacing out departures, due to roster constraints.

It acknowledged this may cause disruptions but added that it was working with airlines to reduce the impact on passenger travel.

“Airservices is enhancing our training pipeline to add further controllers to improve roster depth and is working to address rostering issues that reduce the flexibility of our workforce,” a spokesperson said.

Stephen Beckett, the chief executive of industry group Airlines for Australia and New Zealand, told the ABC on Saturday that Airservices Australia had been unable to roster enough air traffic controllers.

“We’ve just had three days in a row [where] Australia has not been able to roster enough people in the air traffic control centres,” he said.

“They continue to tell us they have recruited enough people to staff the tower. If so, why do we have these persistent problems?” he said.

“The problem in the tower has been going on for years and Australian travellers are having enough of it because these are entirely preventable delays.

“While safety is currently being maintained, it is throwing the schedules out the window and impacting the travelling public. Many people are missing international connections and vital connections to regional Australia.”

Beckett called on Airservices Australia to identify the root cause of the issue and detail plans to address it.

“We need Airservices Australia to support their people and ensure they have enough human resources and other resources to ensure the towers are adequately staffed.”

Sydney airport also faced significant delays on Friday, with some passengers forced to sit on the tarmac for over an hour as more than 120 flights were delayed.

Airservices Australia has previously said air traffic controllers were dedicated to performing a demanding role.

“We take their wellbeing and psychosocial safety seriously and ask that commentary on operational performance recognises the professionalism and commitment of the controllers working every day to keep the travelling public safe.”

The federal transport minister, Catherine King, said on Saturday she had been made aware of disruptions at Sydney airport, attributed to a temporary unavailability of air traffic controllers.

“While a range of measures were put in place to ensure the safe continuation of flights, Airservices needs to do better at managing these disruptions. They cause significant challenges to passengers, staff and airlines,” King said in a statement.

“My office has asked for an explanation and for Airservices to outline a pathway to improve the delivery of its services.”

australia.title: ‘Wet, windy and wintry’: cold front to bring rain and potential flooding to parts of Australia
australia.snippet: Front sweeping across southern Australia expected to bring strong winds and widespread rain over weekend Get our breaking news email , fr...
australia.content:
A vigorous cold front sweeping southern Australia this weekend is forecast to bring damaging winds, rain and potential flooding to parts of the country.

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued severe weather warnings for damaging winds, showers and thunderstorms along Western Australia’s southern coastline on Saturday, and parts of South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales on Sunday. An initial flood watch for river catchments in Victoria and New South Wales was also in place.

A senior meteorologist at the bureau, Ilana Cherny, said it would be a “wet, windy and wintry weekend ahead”.

The front, which was expected to deliver a “cold and icy blast”, would move through WA and SA on Saturday, trailed by gusty winds, showers, thunderstorms and a small chance of hail, Cherny said. A rare dusting of snow was possible atop Bluff Knoll, in WA’s Stirling Range.

Rottnest Island recorded 96km/h winds at 8.54am on Saturday morning.

From Sunday, strong winds, heavy rain and potential storms were expected to reach SA, Victoria and NSW, with wind gusts exceeding 100km/h expected for alpine areas. The BoM has issued warnings for damaging winds across the western Eyre Peninsula and Flinders Ranges in SA, the central and eastern ranges in Victoria and NSW alpine areas.

The front would also bring widespread rain between 20mm and 40mm across southern Australia, with rainfall totals reaching 50mm to 80mm in parts of the south-east.

“With so much rainfall on the way, we are looking at some river level rises to develop later this weekend and into the new week,” Cherny said.

An initial flood watch was in place with river and creek rises and localised flooding possible across river catchments, including the Snowy, Mitchell, Macalister, Bunyip, Yarra, Upper Murray, Mitta Mitta, Kiewa, Ovens, King, Broken, Goulburn rivers and Dandenong Creek.

The cold front would be a “mixed bag” for ski resorts in Victoria and NSW, Cherny said. Plenty of rainfall on Saturday and Sunday was likely to melt pre-existing snow on the mountains but more was expected by Monday.

“With such cold air and plenty of moisture about we could even see a dusting of snow further north through our central tablelands of NSW and even up towards the Barrington Tops,” she said.

Weatherzone’s Anthony Sharwood anticipated multiple bursts of fresh snow through to next Thursday.

“This system has the potential to deliver more than half a metre of fresh snow at elevations around 1,800m, with heavier accumulations possible on the nation’s highest peaks between 1,800m and 2,228m (the height of Mount Kosciuszko).”

After an extremely warm start to the season, the 2026 season was no longer on track for the worst on record, with snow depths at Spencers Creek, NSW, reaching 87.1cm, according to Snowy Hydro – exceeding 85.1cm in 2006, the lowest recorded.

The possibility of snow would increase next week, according to the BoM, with the falls at lower elevations – about 1,000 metres – from around Wednesday.

australia.title: ‘Shame is the punishment’: as Icac delves into the shadowy Reformers, ‘whales’ are coming to the surface
australia.snippet: The corruption watchdog is looking into allegations about Catholic conservative Liberals – but others are getting caught up in the hearin...
australia.content:
“I think they are whale hunting. We just don’t know yet which whale they will hit,” one Liberal insider said after the end of the second week of hearings before the New South Wales Independent Commission against Corruption.

The corruption watchdog is inquiring into allegations a group of young Liberals, known as the Reformers, took illegal donations – including from Catholic Schools NSW, a hotelier, and a fugitive property developer, Jean Nassif – in order to fund branch stacking. The Reformers were intent on gaining control of the Liberal party and ultimately delivering more conservative policies on abortion, euthanasia, marriage equality and climate change.

Property developers and the hotel industry are banned donors in NSW. Donations are also capped and must be declared. All three donors would have breached these requirements – if the donations are found to be political donations.

Some senior Liberals, such as the federal party president, Tony Abbott, this week dismissed the Icac inquiry as an inappropriate probe into standard party shenanigans. But a number of senior figures in the NSW Liberal party are much more worried. Icac inquiries have an uncanny knack of sprawling in unexpected directions.

They fear Icac would not not have spent four years investigating branch stacking and illegal donations by a group of young men unless it was also able to show how the illegal donations infected political decision-making in NSW.

The “whales” of the party whose names have surfaced so far at Icac are the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor; former premier Dominic Perrottet; former NSW finance minister and right power broker Damien Tudehope; and former planning minister Anthony Roberts.

Two other Liberals are also likely to be caught up: the moderate power broker Chris Rath and former fair trading minister Eleni Petinos.

To be clear: none of these people are named as persons of interest in the three published allegations involving breaches of the Electoral Funding Act, and none are under investigation by Icac.

Sometimes Icac doesn’t need to make a finding to demonstrate serious weaknesses in the democratic process. As one Liberal put it: “It’s the shame that is the punishment.”

A rugged two weeks

Before looking at the “whales” and how they surfaced, first, a recap.

In the first two weeks, Icac heard from the most junior of the Reformers. Dylan Whitelaw, now 25, was employed at Catholic Schools NSW in late 2019 after graduating high school that year. He later worked at Beckington, a public relations firm owned by another Reformer, Christian Ellis.

He gave evidence about donations from Catholic Schools and the sort of work he did recruiting young conservatives to the party. In the absence of Ellis, who is in the UK and has declined to return, Whitelaw gave the first insight into some of the money flows.

Icac also heard from another Catholic Schools employee, Rob Assaf, who was more central to the establishment of the Reformers. He gave evidence about the use of fake invoices to disguise payments to the Reformers.

On Wednesday and Thursday, Jean-Claude Perrottet, the 29-year-old brother of the former premier Dominic Perrottet, was in the witness box.

Text messages recovered by Icac indicate Jean-Claude’s role included seeking donations to fund Reformer work from the businessman Frits Maré (who declined) and the hotelier Michael O’Hara, and helping disguise payments through fake invoices. He also was quizzed on texts indicating his job was to work out which branches new members would be stacked into.

Jean-Claude’s evidence also revealed how government positions may have been used to fund the Reformers. At the time Jean-Claude and Ellis were working in Damien Tudehope’s ministerial office as policy advisers. He was grilled about reports they were mainly doing political work, a breach of the ministerial staff rules.

He was questioned about a document which appeared to be a far more extensive plan to place more young Reformer operatives in part-time roles in Liberal MPs’ offices as a way of paying them for branch stacking. The plan included a placement in the premier’s office.

But the bombshell came right at the end of Thursday when Jean-Claude was played a phone intercept of him talking to the developer Nassif, while he was working at Medallion Financial and managing Nassif’s share investments.

Icac alleges Nassif paid three of the Reformers $2m, raising questions about what he wanted in return.

The tapped calls revealed Nassif boasting about getting “the boys” to abolish a Liberal party branch in the seat of the former NSW police minister David Elliott, whom he described as “the worst bulldog bully” and a “lying piece of shit”.

Nassif, whose buildings have been found to be riddled with serious defects, also said in one call: “Take a message to Charlie or to Dom – the building commissioner, we need to stop him. He’s a bully. He’s attacking me left, right and centre.

“I’ve been promised that commissioner will be fucking stopped or changed or fucking done something to him.”

Jean-Claude Perrottet described the call as “crazy talk” and “nonsensical”.

Now to the whales.

Tudehope and the leaked report

During Tudehope’s evidence, he admitted to having introduced O’Hara, a prohibited political donor, to the Reformers and to having some knowledge of their branch recruitment operations.

The biggest revelation came at the end of his evidence when he admitted that he had shared a draft 2023 parliamentary report into the branch stacking by the Reformers in the Hills with one of the men under investigation.

Leaking a draft parliamentary report is a serious breach of parliamentary rules. Tudehope was not on the committee, which raises the question: who gave him the report?

Tudehope has already stepped down from his frontbench position as shadow attorney general, but the leaking will likely spell the end of his political career.

To date, the NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not called for his resignation from the Liberal party – and even indicated prior to his evidence that he could return to the frontbench in the future.

Dominic Perrottet and what he knew

The question that hovers over the inquiry is: what did the former premier Dominic Perrottet know of his siblings’ activity?

His much younger brother has been shown to be an active member of the Reformers. But Charles Perrottet, the brother one down from Dominic in the family of 12 children, is still to give evidence.

Charles has been named as a person of interest in the allegation relating to the $2m from Nassif.

Charles has been Dominic’s political wingman since their days at the University of Sydney, though there are also some who say they have fallen out badly in recent times.

“Joined at the hip,” was how one Liberal described them. “His political sounding board,” said another. “Dom was the singing, dancing frontman. Charles was a really talented political operative in the background.”

Some in the party are particularly concerned by the 2021 cabinet reshuffle that Dominic announced when he became premier. Another phone tap played to the inquiry suggested Nassif had advance warning of the reshuffle, seemingly aware that Petinos would replace the then fair trading minister, Kevin Anderson – and be responsible for the building commissioner.

“I’m gonna step on his neck and strip him from his job,” Nassif was heard saying of the commissioner, David Chandler. “Just give me two months because the consumer affairs minister, she’s gonna be my girl, and the fair trading minister, she’s gonna be one of my girls too, you know?”

After Petinos became fair trading minister, Chandler resigned. In a letter released publicly he cited a breakdown in relations with his minister and concerns about the influence of developers.

When Petinos resigned for unrelated reasons, Chandler was reinstated.

Also a casualty of the reshuffle was the planning minister, Rob Stokes. He was replaced by Anthony Roberts.

Whitelaw, who briefly worked in Roberts’ office while he was planning minister, said Roberts’ chief of staff, Chris Spence, had wanted Petinos to use a video Spence obtained to damage Chandler.

But there were also reasons why Nassif might have been delighted with a change of planning minister.

Before his removal, Stokes had been considering how much density would be permitted on a site near Cherrybrook station that was owned by the state government. Local Liberals said Nassif was not pleased that the site might provide competition to his own developments in the Hills district that were nearing completion.

Matt Kean was also mentioned in a tape as a moderate Nassif believed needed to be pulled into line. Kean had helped Perrottet become premier by delivering moderate numbers. But a reputed deal to make Kean deputy leader was nixed by the right.

Instead, Kean became treasurer and energy minister and the Reformers continued on their mission to take over the party from the moderates.

There have also been suggestions from Tudehope that the premier knew Jean-Claude had gone to Fiji to sit out the parliamentary inquiry into the Hills.

“I went because I was not in a good place and I didn’t want to partake in what I believed was a sham inquiry,” Jean-Claude explained on Thursday.

At the time, Dominic Perrottet indicated he did not know where his brothers were.

Taylor and questions over payments

The involvement – or not – of the federal opposition leader in the Reformers is likely to become clearer next week when the former CEO of Catholic Schools NSW Dallas McInerney gives evidence.

A longtime Liberal power broker, McInerney also was Taylor’s campaign manager in his seat of Hume.

The inquiry has been shown a message from Whitelaw to the Reformers saying: “Dallas has told me he got the commitment from Angus for the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation.”

Taylor said last week: “No payment was made.”

This careful form of words does not rule out the possibility that Taylor promised financial support for the Reformers, but withdrew it. There was a hint in Jean-Claude’s evidence that Taylor had a dislike for one of the Reformers, Assaf.

Branch stacking and the power of the right

As one senior Liberal said of the portrait of the right of the party that is emerging at Icac: “This is not John Howard’s right.”

By the end of the second week, we have learned how a very conservative sub-faction of the right worked to dominate the Liberal party in NSW.

A year ago the NSW Liberals installed Sloane as the new leader, in an effort to save as many seats as possible, as they battled the headwinds of a deeply dysfunctional federal Liberal party.

The thinking was Sloane was a better communicator than her predecessor, Mark Speakman, who would be able to differentiate the NSW Liberals from their federal colleagues.

Her job was to sell the message that, at state level, the Liberals were a modern party in touch with the broad community and its concerns about cost of living, that it was a party that believed in climate action, and that it was welcoming of minorities.

But the news that the right may now control branches through these stacking activities will undercut that message.

The South Australian and Western Australian Liberal parties have already seen takeovers by religiously aligned rightwing cooperatives. The result has been they have been reduced to a handful of seats in their state parliaments.

The NSW Liberals would be well advised to look at those examples and deal with the aftermath of the stacking as soon as possible.

australia.title: Senior managers at St Basil’s aged care, where 50 died from Covid, can’t remember it all. Grieving loved ones can’t forget
australia.snippet: Konstantin Kontis and Vicky Kos were compelled to testify at a coronial inquest resuming on the sixth anniversary of the tragedy Get our ...
australia.content:
Quiet sobs could be heard in Melbourne’s coroner’s court, as several families attended to finally hear from the pair who were the most senior managers when, throughout July and August 2020, almost a quarter of the 188 residents at St Basil’s aged care home died from Covid-19 or neglect.

Following multiple failed legal bids to avoid giving evidence after 50 residents died in the Victorian aged care home they managed, Konstantin Kontis and Vicky Kos were compelled to testify at a coronial inquest resuming on the sixth anniversary of the tragedy.

During his evidence on Friday, Kontis said that the board of St Basil’s, operating under the auspice of the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia, never signed off on the facility’s Covid-19 management policy and that he believed, as chair, he had the delegated authority to approve it without them.

Counsel assisting the coroner, Naomi Hodgson, told the court the policy contained no strong guidance on close contacts of Covid cases, and that the main guidance on symptoms was to follow the directives of the state and federal governments.

The policy document was not updated as new directives came in from the government, the court heard. Instead this information was printed and put into a yellow folder for staff to keep up-to-date with.

Kontis accepted under questioning that there was no delegation of authority that allowed him to approve “such a significant document” without input from the board.

Kontis was also questioned about why he did not convene board meetings as the outbreak grew, especially once testing of 116 residents and 95 staff on 15 July 2020 – as organised by the federal department of health – revealed 28 positive cases.

“My communication then had switched to the archbishop direct,” Kontis said.

“I don’t want to put tickets on myself, but he had full confidence that I would handle the matter in the most appropriate way.”

Hodgson put it to Kontis that regardless of whether an approved aged care provider was a not-for-profit, for-profit, or religiously run, the leadership had obligations under the aged care and corporate laws to inform the board.

She suggested Kontis was wrong in some of his understanding of these obligations, which he accepted.

Kontis said a board meeting was held in April 2020 before the outbreak at the home and after Covid was spreading through aged care elsewhere. Discussions would have occurred then, he said, about what to do if a significant portion of the workforce became infected.

The court heard that no minutes from that meeting had been found in about 10,000 pages of briefing evidence provided to the coroner. It prompted the inquest – due to close its questioning of witnesses on Friday – to be delayed to allow St Basil’s representatives to conduct a search.

Kontis’ evidence is due to resume on 16 November.

The yellow folder

Earlier in the week, the court heard that no cohort plan for separating Covid positive residents from uninfected ones could be found in documents provided to the court.

Kos, who was director of nursing and facility manager at the time, said this plan was placed in the yellow folder. Some documents from that folder had gone missing, she said.

She gave evidence that many documents from the state and federal government were being added to this folder, and that staff were expected to keep up-to-date with it when starting shifts. Information was also shared during handovers, she said.

Following this evidence, a search on Monday night of electronic and hard-file repositories of documents, including those previously seized by Victoria police, did not reveal such a cohort plan, the court heard on Tuesday from St Basil’s barrister, Conor O’Bryan.

O’Bryan said because some files had been lost it could not be proven that a cohort plan never existed.

‘I didn’t attend’

During his evidence, Kontis was pressed on why he did not attend key meetings, organised by senior management of the home and attended by health officials, once it became clear the outbreak was significant and the entire workforce needed to be stood down.

Kontis said he disagreed with a directive from the chief health officer at the time, Prof Brett Sutton, to furlough the entire workforce and replace them with agency staff to prevent further spread. Kontis said he did not trust the staff would be competent and Covid-free.

“You’ve just received the news that your entire staff is going to be stood down,” Hodgson said. “Why didn’t you attend [meetings] as the only person on the board with vision of what was happening here?”

Kontis responded: “I can’t answer that. I didn’t attend.” He said he was informed about what happened at meetings immediately afterwards by attenders.

Kontis said there were also some meetings he did not believe he was invited to.

Hodgson said that St Basil’s, as an approved aged care provider, had a duty under law to implement policies and procedures to manage risk and ensure care for consumers.

Asked why he did not convene a meeting of the risk and audit committee before or throughout the outbreak, Kontis said, “I couldn’t get anybody to attend a meeting because of Covid.”

Hodgson responded this was “an improbable answer in circumstances where you’ve already told me you can get people on the phone”.

The court previously heard that agency staff brought in to take over struggled to find the information they needed to run the facility, from passwords and logins for computers, to notes about the clinical care of residents.

Kontis said this information could be found in folders. “We had folders in the kitchen, folders with the cleaners, folders with the maintenance people,” he said.

Hodgson put it to Kontis that, as an approved aged care provider and chairman, he had responsibility for the agency staff and to assist them to fulfil their duties.

“Well, that’s your interpretation,” Kontis said.

Hodgson replied: “I’d suggest to you … that it’s not my interpretation, it was your responsibility as an approved provider.”

“That’s that’s your assertion,” Kontis said.

Signs in ‘simple language’

Kos had earlier told the court that English was a second language for 95% of the original St Basil’s staff, and the majority did not have laptops or computers. Asked how critical and sometimes complicated Covid information was then communicated, she said signs in “simple language” were placed around the facility and information was shared during shift handovers.

Kos disagreed under cross-examination that the process of adding documents constantly to folders and expecting staff with English as a second language to keep across these during shifts was a complex task for them.

She agreed that having a clear Covid plan in place would make it less likely that people would die.

The inquest had previously heard from staff and family members in 2021 that infected residents were mingling with those who had not tested positive to the virus, and that infection control procedures throughout the home were poor.

Kos told the court that on 9 July 2020, when the first case in a staff member was identified, she began to follow a Covid-19 aged care checklist issued by the federal government about what to do in the first 24 hours.

Kos told the court she did not complete the step that said to alert the commonwealth department of health at a dedicated aged care email address within 30 minutes.

She said she spoke with the state public health hotline as the document required, and because she was told to wait to hear about next steps, she did not proceed to the next step on the checklist, which was to email the commonwealth.

The checklist said the commonwealth could connect aged care homes with resources to manage the outbreak including testing, additional PPE and a surge workforce, the court heard.

Delays in the commonwealth learning of the case meant staff and residents were not mass-tested until days later. The inquest previously heard this was a root cause of the outbreak.

Kontis said he did not believe it was his role to email the commonwealth as he trusted facility staff to do so and to follow procedures in place.

‘I don’t remember’

Throughout the five days, Kontis had to be reminded several times not to interject during questioning, and to listen before responding. With years having passed since the tragedy, Kos’ response to many questions throughout the week was, “I don’t remember”.

Both Kontis and Kos refused to testify, only doing so after a certificate was granted by the coroner, Liberty Sanger – meaning their evidence can not be used against them in criminal or civil litigation.

Spiros Vasilakis, whose mother, Maria, died at the home during the outbreak, attended each day.

“It still hurts for all of us families here,” Vasilakis said.

“It hurts to hear anyone say that because it’s been six years, they can’t remember. I can tell you that families remember, detail by detail, what occurred. I haven’t forgotten anything.”

The inquest continues.

australia.title: David Brat bound for Australia as diplomat confirmed as next US ambassador
australia.snippet: Former Republican state congressman, who once argued Christianity and capitalism should merge, confirmed by US Senate to fill long-vacant...
australia.content:
Former Virginia congressman David Brat has been confirmed by the US Senate to be the next US ambassador to Australia, after the role had been left vacant for 18 months.

Brat’s confirmation was among more than 70 votes pushed through the Senate by Republicans on Friday, Washington time, before the summer recess.

Brat was nominated by Donald Trump in April. The 61-year-old served two terms in Congress until 2018, when he was defeated by a Democrat, and was vice-president of business relations at Virginia’s Liberty University.

The ambassador role had been vacant since November 2024, when Joe Biden’s ambassador, Caroline Kennedy, left the post.

Anthony Albanese in April said he would work with anyone Trump nominated, when asked to respond to Brat’s earlier claims that US intelligence agencies conspired to remove Trump from office.

“We respect the sovereignty of countries to put forward ambassadors just like we expect our choices to be endorsed,” he said at the time.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, welcomed Brat’s appointment in a statement on Saturday.

“He will find Australia to be a warm host and a good friend,” she said. “We share his priorities of critical minerals, defence cooperation and partnership in the Indo-Pacific. Together we will strengthen the alliance in the interests of both our countries.”

The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, told reporters on Saturday it was important to have the position now filled.

“The bilateral relationship is of course a deeply important one and we welcome the appointment of the new ambassador.”

Brat was described by Time magazine in 2010 as a “Tea Party professor” and an enthusiast of the author Ayn Rand.

In a 2011 paper, he argued that capitalism and Christianity should merge, writing: “If we all did the right thing and had the guts to spread the word, we would not need the government to backstop every action we take.”

Brat was swept into the Senate in 2014 when he defeated the then House of Representatives majority leader, Eric Cantor, in a primary. He lost his seat in 2018 to Democrat Abigail Spanberger, who is now the governor of Virginia.

The confirmation comes amid tense US-Australia relations, with Trump levelling 12.5% tariffs on many Australian exports in July. Australia was on a list of 54 economies hit with the tariffs due to what the US claimed was a failure “to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”.

At the time, the trade minister, Don Farrell, called for the tariffs to be removed, saying they were inconsistent with Australia’s free-trade agreement with the US.

Brat’s arrival in Australia will coincide with the 75th anniversary of the Anzus treaty, a security pact over defence of the Pacific, and comes after the Albanese government announced in May it would instead buy three second-hand American nuclear submarines as part of the $370bn Aukus deal, instead of two second-hand and one new as originally intended.

While the Albanese government has remained supportive of Aukus, there has been growing disquiet from some within Labor about the plan. Former cabinet minister Ed Husic said in June that the change meant “we are not going to get the deal that was promised to us”.

The former defence secretary Greg Moriarty has been Australia’s representative in Washington since taking over from former prime minister Kevin Rudd in April.

world.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
world.snippet: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce tempora...
world.content:
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

world.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
world.snippet: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians Temporary protected status...
world.content:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

Meanwhile, in a statement to the Guardian on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention, and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. Those ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
world.snippet: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation The virus causing a ma...
world.content:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

world.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
world.snippet: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon The US state department is to shu...
world.content:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

world.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
world.snippet: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone The Ugandan football comm...
world.content:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”
